doc.title: Ray Drummond interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Jazz education versus the commercial convention
summary: Asked about the jazz educators convention, he discusses the tension between education and media commerce and between educators and professionals, and his return to teaching after 25 years.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Is this whole thing here with the jazz convention and jazz education, is that in any way messing with the evolution?
No. You’re talking about the convention itself?
I’m talking about the concept I guess of — gosh I guess teaching jazz in a college.

No, no. None of that. No, no. There are two issues with this convention. I’m not sure — first of all you have to understand I’m a political sociologist. That’s my degree. That’s what my undergraduate degree was really in. And so I see two specific missions that aren’t necessarily compatible that are not exclusive and they don’t conflict with one another but they have parts of each other that do conflict. Okay on the one hand this convention and this organization is about jazz education okay? But on the other hand this © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

convention has now taken on an additional responsibility, especially now since the Jazz Times convention folded or actually more accurately has folded a small portion of itself into this particular convention. So you’ve got really a pull between the commercial forces of the media, of the entertainment industry, meaning the record companies and other media companies that are interested in the commercial media. You’ve got them pulling at the educational because they’re trying to get them to feed them and yet there is a certain kind of dynamic that exists in jazz education because as you know there has always been kind of a hidden war — it’s not war but a hidden conflict between the musicians, professional musicians, and the educators which is really unfortunate. It’s really ridiculous. Because everybody’s trying to do the exact same thing, which is to make the pie bigger for the jazz community. I mean the musicians not only are they looking for more venues but they’re looking for audience. The universities have the perfect opportunity to not only have musicians in music programs and whatnot but to actually be a place where future audiences can actually learn something about jazz, classical music, folk music, world music, whatever. And then as they go out to work, become lawyers, doctors, dentists, police officers, whatever, diplomats, the point is that they have been exposed to other things and they begin to make quote informed choices you know. So to me it’s obvious that the mission for both camps is exactly the same. But somewhere along the line you’ve got some people who actually say oh you’re an educator, oh. You’re not as good as a professional. Or a professional saying well you’re an educator so you don’t think I’m as good as you. It’s like wait a minute guys. It’s very specious as far as I’m concerned, that part of it. So you have that happening, that’s traditional, that’s been part of this organization, that’s part of the baggage that this organization has always carried with it, and then now you’ve also grafted this other media hype business that has got more muscle and more money in one sense because it’s more dynamic. So at least — and it’s also the one that’s tied in to youthful notions of what it means to be quote successful unquote. Because success, we know, really doesn’t have much to do — it has somewhat to do with commercial success — but that’s not what we really as educators or as professionals, jazz lovers, are looking for. It’s not so much most musicians I don’t think come into jazz music because I’m going to make a killing, I’m going to be the next Rockefeller, I’m going to be the next thing, I’m going to be the next Beatles. I mean you know it’s not on that level. It’s usually I have this passion for this music that I’ve always loved, it’s nurtured me, it’s gotten me through hard times and more importantly it’s something that I just feel compelled to actually be in this community and to try to one acquire and develop and deepen this voice that I think I hear or feel or however it appears to you. And I think that this is the mission of educators as well. I think people that really — I mean I have to be very candid in how I feel about education because for the first © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

time in 25 years I’m back now in an institutional setting as a faculty member and I’m really enjoying it again. But then I knew I would because I like teaching. But I took myself off the market for 25 years because I wanted to be fully a professional musician. I didn’t want — it wasn’t that it was a problem being an educator it’s just that I wanted to see what it was going to be like for me to be out there earning my own living without an institution behind me, without any of the — I mean it’s not a safety net, it’s just a different way of being employed. It’s a different relationship. You’re still working for yourself but you have another kind of relationship that you have to nurture. And the political aspects of being in the educational establishment, I mean that’s a whole other thing. I mean it’s similar to what you have to do and the political aspects of your career as a professional musician. But it’s a different — I mean it’s a different institutional setting.
